context: The input is [7, 3, 2, 6, 0, 1, 5, 4]. Each split divides the array in half by position, regardless of the values. Splitting stops when a subarray has length 1 because a single element is already sorted.

frames.explanation: In the upper half, three levels of splits produce 8 single-element subarrays, triggering the base case. In the lower half, the subarrays are merged in pairs from the bottom up. Each merge starts with two subarrays already sorted in ascending order. Compare the first remaining element on each side and place the smaller one in the output range. When one side runs out, append the rest of the other side. This keeps each merged result sorted. The crossing arrows in the lower half trace where each element goes in the next merged result. They do not represent pairwise swaps in place.
frames.title: Splitting and merging in merge sort

result: The figure shows data dependencies side by side at each level of the recursion tree. The code in this section processes the entire left branch, then the right branch, and finally merges their results.
summary: Recursively split the array at its midpoint until each subarray contains one element. Then merge adjacent sorted subarrays level by level to obtain the complete sorted array.
